(CNN)  -- Over 28,000 Liverpool fans marked the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster in a special memorial service at Anfield on Wednesday. Liverpool supporters at the Kop end paid their respects in an emotional afternoon at Anfield. A total of 96 supporters died on April 15, 1989 before the FA Cup semifinal between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday's stadium, the worst-ever tragedy in English sporting history. To commemorate the anniversary, the city of Liverpool came to a standstill at 3.06 pm (1406 GMT) with the bells of the two cathedrals and its civic buildings ringing out in memory of those fans who lost their lives. On Anfield's famous Kop, 96 candles were lit while commemorations took place at Hillsborough and also in Nottingham. Members of the current Liverpool team stood somberly as hymns were played before a roll call of the dead was read out. Club legend Kenny Dalglish, who was Liverpool manager at the time of the disaster, then read a short prayer. The mayor of Liverpool, Steve Rotherham, who was at the game 20 years ago, helped organize the emotional memorial. "Hillsborough affected so many lives, not just on Merseyside but across the whole of the UK," he said. "I attended the match 20 years ago and the passing years do not diminish the importance and the poignancy of this occasion." Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard, whose 10-year-old cousin Jon-Paul Gilhooley was the youngest victim of the tragedy, spoke of his feelings this week. "Time has gone by, but the scars will never ever be healed and the fans will never ever forget. So you can always rely on our supporters to be there for you when you need them." The Liverpool fans died in a crush which started just before the kick-off as the gate at the Leppings Lane End was opened with terrible consequences. The match started but when the scale of the tragedy became clear, it was swiftly abandoned at 3.06 pm. In the immediate aftermath, the British government commissioned Lord Justice Taylor to conduct an inquiry which would have a far-reaching impact on football. Taylor was deeply critical of the police operation at Hillsborough, but his most significant recommendations were the removal of perimeter fencing and the creation of all-seater stadia. His report also cleared Liverpool fans of blame for the tragedy after lurid tabloid headlines provoked revulsion on Merseyside. Prime minister Gordon Brown paid reference to the controversy in an interview released on Liverpool's official television channel. "It was wrong for people to blame, as some did, Liverpool fans on that day," he said. "That's probably what matters most -- that people understood that the behavior of Liverpool fans in helping each other was magnificent. "Let's never forget the fans who cruelly lost their lives on a day when we know the people of Liverpool were trying to help each other," he added. However, the people of Liverpool are still angry and bitter at the lack of justice for those who died -- and that frustration surfaced when Andy Burnham, the   Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport took to the stand to address the crowd. As Burnham spoke, the crowd rose as one to sing "Justice for the 96". The Kop chant boomed around the stadium and Burnham, an Everton fan, was left in no doubt about the strength of feeling over the lack of accountability from officialdom over the tragedy. Fittingly, the ceremony was concluded with Gerry Marsden leading the fans in singing Liverpool anthem 'You'll Never Walk Alone'.

**Liverpool Falls Silent 20 Years After Hillsborough**

*By Staff Reporter*  
*Liverpool, April 15, 2009*

Liverpool paused today to mark the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster, a tragedy that claimed the lives of 96 men, women and children and left an indelible wound on the city, its football club and the nation’s conscience.

At 3.06pm — the time the 1989 FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest was stopped — the city fell silent. Traffic slowed, public transport paused, shops and offices observed two minutes’ silence, and church bells rang out across Merseyside. On the River Mersey, ferry horns sounded in tribute. Flags flew at half-mast as Liverpool remembered those who went to a football match and never came home.

The anniversary was marked most poignantly at Anfield, where thousands gathered for an emotional memorial service at the home of Liverpool Football Club. Families of the victims, survivors, supporters, former players, civic leaders and representatives of the wider football community filled the stadium in a ceremony defined by grief, remembrance and the continuing demand for justice.

## The Disaster of 1989

On April 15, 1989, Liverpool met Nottingham Forest in an FA Cup semi-final at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield, the neutral venue then used regularly for major fixtures. As kick-off approached, severe congestion built up outside the Leppings Lane end, where Liverpool supporters had been allocated standing terraces.

In an attempt to ease the crush outside the ground, police opened an exit gate, allowing a large number of fans to enter. Many were funnelled into already overcrowded central pens behind the goal. With perimeter fencing preventing escape onto the pitch, supporters were crushed against barriers and against one another.

The match began at 3pm but was halted six minutes later as the scale of the disaster became apparent. Supporters tore down advertising hoardings to use as makeshift stretchers; others tried desperately to pull people from the packed terraces. In the chaos that followed, 94 people were initially confirmed dead. The number later rose to 95, and then 96, after Tony Bland died in 1993 from injuries sustained at Hillsborough.

The victims ranged in age from 10 to 67. Among them were children, parents, siblings and friends — ordinary supporters who had travelled to watch their team in one of English football’s biggest matches.

## The Taylor Report and Football’s Transformation

In the aftermath, Lord Justice Taylor was appointed to lead a public inquiry. His interim report, published in August 1989, rejected early attempts to blame supporters and instead identified a failure of police control as the main cause of the disaster.

Taylor’s final report, published in 1990, reshaped English football. It recommended the removal of perimeter fencing and the conversion of major stadiums to all-seater venues. The report led to sweeping safety reforms across the game, transforming the experience of watching football in Britain.

Yet for many families, the Taylor Report was only the beginning. They continued to campaign against what they saw as official failures, misinformation and an incomplete accounting of what happened before, during and after the disaster. By the 20th anniversary, that fight for full disclosure and accountability remained central to Hillsborough’s legacy.

## Liverpool’s Citywide Tribute

Across Liverpool today, the anniversary was observed not simply as a football remembrance but as a civic act of mourning. The disaster’s impact has long extended beyond Anfield and beyond Liverpool supporters; it is woven into the identity of the city itself.

At municipal buildings, flags were lowered. Schools, workplaces and public services marked the silence. The streets, usually busy in the afternoon, briefly stilled as people stopped where they were — on pavements, in offices, at stations and in shops — to remember the 96.

For many in Liverpool, Hillsborough remains a shared sorrow: a loss carried by families directly affected, by survivors who live with trauma, and by a city that has spent two decades insisting that the dead should be remembered with dignity and truth.

## Anfield Memorial: Grief, Defiance and Song

The focus of the day was Anfield, where the Kop and the stands filled for the annual memorial service, made especially significant by the passage of 20 years. The names of the 96 were read aloud, each one met with solemn applause and quiet reflection. Candles were lit in their memory, and floral tributes surrounded the Hillsborough memorial outside the stadium.

The service included prayers, hymns and addresses from religious and civic figures. Liverpool players and officials joined families on the pitch, while supporters held scarves aloft in a familiar gesture of unity and remembrance.

There were tears throughout the stadium as families listened to the names of their loved ones. Many wore red scarves or carried photographs. Banners demanding justice were visible in the stands, a reminder that grief and protest have never been separate in the story of Hillsborough.

The ceremony closed with the anthem that has become inseparable from Liverpool Football Club and from the families’ long campaign: **“You’ll Never Walk Alone.”** As it rang around Anfield, thousands joined in, the song carrying both sorrow and resolve.

Twenty years on, the memories of April 15, 1989 remain painfully vivid. But today’s commemorations also showed the enduring solidarity of a city that has refused to forget.

**The 96 were remembered not as numbers, but as lives — and as part of Liverpool’s history forever.**
